The patient presents with a classic triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and cognitive/speech changes, but also features rigidity, tremor, and orthostatic hypotension. This constellation of symptoms, particularly the combination of parkinsonism (rigidity, tremor) and autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension, incontinence) with relatively early gait instability, strongly suggests Multiple System Atrophy (MSA), specifically the parkinsonian subtype (MSA-P), or potentially Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP). However, the prominent autonomic features and urinary issues point more strongly toward MSA. Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) is a differential for the triad but doesn't explain the rigidity/tremor/autonomic issues as well. Parkinson's disease usually has later autonomic involvement.
